statement speaks of the division given, and every division gives the same sum
(`Apart.area_eq_of_same_region`).

propositions.statement: ∀ {E₁ E E₂ : Elements.Point} (F : Elements.Figures.Outline), Elements.Triangle E₁ E E₂ → Exists fun (K : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (P : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (L : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (M : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.Parallelogram K P L M) (And (Eq (Elements.ang P K M) (Elements.ang E₁ E E₂)) (Eq (Elements.quadArea K P L M) (Elements.Figures.Outline.area F)))
propositions.name: BookI.Prop45.outline
propositions.enunciation:
**I.45, for a figure given by its outline** (companion of I.45, certificate name I.45
outline; the proposition in general). To construct, in a given rectilineal angle E, a
parallelogram KPLM, its angle at K equal to E, equal to a given rectilineal figure: the
figure given by its outline alone (`Outline`), with any number of sides, and holes, separate
pieces or contacts at corners if it has them; and "equal to the figure" meaning equal to its
area (`Outline.area`), which every division of it gives. The division is obtained by a
theorem (`division_exists`), Euclid's construction applied to its triangles
(`Prop45.apart`), and their sum is the outline's area (`area_eq`).

propositions.statement: ∀ {E₁ E E₂ : Elements.Point} (ts : List (Prod Elements.Point (Prod Elements.Point Elements.Point))), Ne ts List.nil → (∀ (t : Prod Elements.Point (Prod Elements.Point Elements.Point)), Membership.mem ts t → Elements.Triangle (Prod.fst t) (Prod.fst (Prod.snd t)) (Prod.snd (Prod.snd t))) → Elements.Triangle E₁ E E₂ → Exists fun (K : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (F : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (L : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (M : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.Parallelogram K F L M) (And (Eq (Elements.ang F K M) (Elements.ang E₁ E E₂)) (Eq (Elements.quadArea K F L M) (Elements.Magnitude.sum (List.map (fun (t : Prod Elements.Point (Prod Elements.Point Elements.Point)) => Elements.area (Prod.fst t) (Prod.fst (Prod.snd t)) (Prod.snd (Prod.snd t))) ts))))
propositions.name: BookI.Prop45.sum
propositions.enunciation:
**I.45, any number of triangles** (companion of I.45). To construct, in a given
rectilineal angle E, a parallelogram equal to any number of given triangles taken together,
at least one: I.42 for the first, then `Prop45.append` for each of the rest, in order. The
triangles are any triangles, each with its corners off one straight line; they need not fit
together into one figure, and the statement claims nothing of a figure.

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B C D E F G H K : Elements.Point}, Elements.Triangle A B C → Eq (Elements.ang B A C) Elements.rightAngle → Elements.Square B D E C → Elements.SameSideOf D E B C → Elements.Square A B F G → Elements.SameSideOf F G A B → Elements.Square A C K H → Elements.SameSideOf K H A C → Eq (Elements.quadArea B D E C) (HAdd.hAdd (Elements.quadArea A B F G) (Elements.quadArea A C K H))
propositions.name: BookI.Prop47.general
propositions.enunciation:
The area identity for squares on either side of each base. Each square's far
corners lie together on one side of its base, with no prescribed side relative to
the triangle or to the other squares.

We construct outward squares by I.46, apply `Prop47`, and transfer the result by
`Prop46.square_eq`, since squares on the same base have equal areas. Euclid's
angle-addition argument remains in the outward configuration.

propositions.statement: ∀ {A₁ A₂ B : Elements.Point} {ps : List Elements.Point}, Elements.InOrder (List.cons B ps) → Eq (Elements.rect A₁ A₂ B (Elements.endOf B ps)) (Elements.Magnitude.sum (List.map (fun (s : Prod Elements.Point Elements.Point) => Elements.rect A₁ A₂ (Prod.fst s) (Prod.snd s)) (Elements.segments (List.cons B ps))))
propositions.name: BookII.Prop1.general
propositions.enunciation:
**II.1, any number of segments** (companion of II.1). If the straight line from B to its
end is cut at any number of points in order, the rectangle contained by A₁A₂ and the whole
is equal to the rectangles contained by A₁A₂ and each of the segments. The list `ps` is
the points of section followed by the end; with no points of section it is the whole
straight line alone, and with no points at all the straight line is nothing and so is each
side.

propositions.statement: ∀ {A₁ A₂ B C D : Elements.Point}, Elements.Between B D C → Eq (Elements.rect A₁ A₂ B C) (HAdd.hAdd (Elements.rect A₁ A₂ B D) (Elements.rect A₁ A₂ D C))
propositions.name: BookII.Prop1.two
propositions.enunciation:
**II.1, one cut** (companion of II.1). If the straight line BC is cut at D, the
rectangle contained by A₁A₂ and BC is equal to the rectangles contained by A₁A₂ and each
of BD, DC. II.1's construction, with one parallel drawn through D. The uncut straight line
A₁A₂ may be nothing, and then every rectangle is nothing.

propositions.statement: ∀ (R : Elements.Apart), Exists fun (P : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (Q : Elements.Point) => Eq (Elements.sq P Q) (Elements.Apart.area R)
propositions.name: BookII.Prop14.apart
propositions.enunciation:
**II.14, for a figure given with triangles that do not overlap** (companion of II.14). To
construct a square equal to a given rectilineal figure, given with a checked division into
triangles, any division of it whose triangles lie apart, no point inside two of them
(`Apart`), as in `Prop45.apart`: the square on PQ is equal to those triangles taken together
(`Apart.area`). The figure may have a hole, touch itself at a corner, or be in more than one
piece. It is `Prop14.sum` for the figure's
triangles. As in `Prop45.apart`, the statement speaks of the division given, and every
division gives the same sum (`Apart.area_eq_of_same_region`).

propositions.statement: ∀ {A₀ A₁ A₂ : Elements.Point} {ps : List Elements.Point}, (∀ (s : Prod Elements.Point Elements.Point), Membership.mem (Elements.segments (List.cons A₁ (List.cons A₂ ps))) s → Elements.Triangle A₀ (Prod.fst s) (Prod.snd s)) → (∀ (t : Prod Elements.Point (Prod Elements.Point Elements.Point)), Membership.mem (Elements.triples (List.cons A₁ (List.cons A₂ ps))) t → Elements.OppositeSidesOf (Prod.fst t) (Prod.snd (Prod.snd t)) A₀ (Prod.fst (Prod.snd t))) → LT.lt (Elements.Magnitude.sum (List.map (fun (s : Prod Elements.Point Elements.Point) => Elements.ang (Prod.fst s) A₀ (Prod.snd s)) (Elements.segments (List.cons A₁ (List.cons A₂ ps))))) (HAdd.hAdd (HAdd.hAdd Elements.rightAngle Elements.rightAngle) (HAdd.hAdd Elements.rightAngle Elements.rightAngle)) → Exists fun (R : Elements.Rectilineal) => And (Eq (Elements.Rectilineal.pieces R) (List.map (fun (s : Prod Elements.Point Elements.Point) => Prod.mk A₀ (Prod.mk (Prod.fst s) (Prod.snd s))) (Elements.segments (List.cons A₁ (List.cons A₂ ps))))) (Exists fun (P : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (Q : Elements.Point) => Eq (Elements.sq P Q) (Elements.Rectilineal.area R))
propositions.name: BookII.Prop14.fan
propositions.enunciation:
**II.14, for a figure divided from one corner** (companion of II.14), as Euclid and
Oliver Byrne divide it. A figure with corners A₀, A₁, A₂, …, Aₙ, divided by the straight
lines from A₀ into the triangles A₀A₁A₂, …, A₀Aₙ₋₁Aₙ, with the division checked as in
`Prop45.fan`: each piece a triangle, each two neighbouring triangles on opposite sides of
the straight line A₀Aᵢ they share, and the angles at A₀ together less than four right
angles. Then those triangles, in that order, are fitted together into one figure
(`Fitted.fan`), and the square on PQ is equal to that figure, that is, to the triangles
taken together. The figure is the one with corners A₀, A₁, …, Aₙ in order round it, bounded
by that closed line (`Prop45.fan_boundary`), and the triangles' sum is its area, the same for
every division of it (`area_eq`). The square drawn is `Prop14.square R.toApart`, for the
glued figure R returned.

As in `Prop45.fan`, the first conclusion is what the two conditions are for; the square
alone would follow from each piece being a triangle, by `Prop14.sum`.

propositions.statement: ∀ (R : Elements.Rectilineal), Exists fun (P : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (Q : Elements.Point) => Eq (Elements.sq P Q) (Elements.Rectilineal.area R)
propositions.name: BookII.Prop14.figure
propositions.enunciation:
**II.14, for a figure with one boundary, given with triangles fitted together**
(companion of II.14). To construct a square equal to a given rectilineal figure, given with
a checked division into triangles, fitted together in a suitable order, each glued across a
side of an earlier one and meeting the earlier ones only along it (`Rectilineal`), as in
`Prop45.figure`: the square on PQ is equal to those triangles taken together
(`Rectilineal.area`). It is `Prop14.apart` for the figure's
triangles, which lie apart (`Fitted.inside_pairwise`, `Rectilineal.toApart`), and every
division gives the same sum (`Apart.area_eq_of_same_region`).

propositions.statement: ∀ (F : Elements.Figures.Outline), Exists fun (P : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (Q : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (S : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (T : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.Square P Q S T) (And (Elements.Parallelogram P Q S T) (Eq (Elements.quadArea P Q S T) (Elements.Figures.Outline.area F)))
propositions.name: BookII.Prop14.outline
propositions.enunciation:
**II.14, for a figure given by its outline** (companion of II.14, certificate name II.14
outline; the proposition in general). To construct a square PQST, drawn, equal to a given
rectilineal figure: the figure given by its outline alone (`Outline`), as in
`Prop45.outline`, and "equal to the figure" meaning equal to its area (`Outline.area`), which
every division of it gives. The square is a parallelogram. The division is obtained by a
theorem (`division_exists`), Euclid's rectangle and then its square are made for its
triangles (`Prop14.square`), and their sum is the outline's area (`area_eq`).

propositions.statement: ∀ (F : Elements.Figures.Outline), Exists fun (P : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (Q : Elements.Point) => Eq (Elements.sq P Q) (Elements.Figures.Outline.area F)
propositions.name: BookII.Prop14.outline_side
propositions.enunciation:
**II.14, the side, for a figure given by its outline** (companion of II.14, certificate
name II.14 outline_side). The side form of `Prop14.outline`: a straight line PQ whose square
equals the outline's area, from a division (`division_exists`), the side found for its
triangles (`Prop14.apart`), and the content theorem (`area_eq`).

propositions.statement: ∀ {E B C D : Elements.Point}, Elements.Rectangle E B C D → Exists fun (P : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (Q : Elements.Point) => Eq (Elements.sq P Q) (Elements.quadArea E B C D)
propositions.name: BookII.Prop14.rectangle
propositions.enunciation:
**II.14, for a rectangle** (companion of II.14). To construct a square equal to a given
rectangle EBCD: the second part of Euclid's proof, with both of its cases. If BE is equal to
ED, the rectangle is a square already. If not, the greater, say BE, is produced to F with EF
equal to ED, BF is bisected at G, the semicircle BHF is described with centre G, and DE is
produced to H; then the rectangle BE, EF with the square on EG is the square on GF [II. 5],
which is the squares on HE, EG [I. 47], and the rectangle is the square on EH. This is
the proof of `Prop14` after the rectangle is made, written out again so that it need not
cite II.14. The square is the square on PQ.

propositions.statement: ∀ (R : Elements.Apart), Exists fun (P : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (Q : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (S : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (T : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.Square P Q S T) (And (Elements.Parallelogram P Q S T) (Eq (Elements.quadArea P Q S T) (Elements.Apart.area R)))
propositions.name: BookII.Prop14.square
propositions.enunciation:
**II.14, with the square drawn** (companion of II.14). To construct a square PQST equal
to a given rectilineal figure, given with a checked division into triangles that lie apart,
as in `Prop14.apart`: the square on the side that `Prop14.apart` finds, described on it
[I. 46]. The square is a
parallelogram, and it is equal to the figure's triangles taken together. A figure R given
by gluing (`Rectilineal`) is taken here as `R.toApart`, the same triangles, which lie apart,
with the same sum (`Rectilineal.area_toApart`); so is the glued figure that `Prop14.fan`
returns for a checked fan.

propositions.statement: ∀ (ts : List (Prod Elements.Point (Prod Elements.Point Elements.Point))), Ne ts List.nil → (∀ (t : Prod Elements.Point (Prod Elements.Point Elements.Point)), Membership.mem ts t → Elements.Triangle (Prod.fst t) (Prod.fst (Prod.snd t)) (Prod.snd (Prod.snd t))) → Exists fun (P : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (Q : Elements.Point) => Eq (Elements.sq P Q) (Elements.Magnitude.sum (List.map (fun (t : Prod Elements.Point (Prod Elements.Point Elements.Point)) => Elements.area (Prod.fst t) (Prod.fst (Prod.snd t)) (Prod.snd (Prod.snd t))) ts))
propositions.name: BookII.Prop14.sum
propositions.enunciation:
**II.14, any number of triangles** (companion of II.14). To construct a square equal to
any number of given triangles taken together, at least one: a rectangle equal to them
[I. 45, `Prop45.sum`, in a right angle from I.11 at a corner A of the first triangle ABC, on
AB], then a square equal to the rectangle (`Prop14.rectangle`). The triangles are any
triangles; they need not fit together into one figure, and the statement claims nothing of
a figure. The square is the square on PQ.

propositions.statement: ∀ {A D E F : Elements.Point} {ABCD : Elements.Circle}, Elements.Centre E ABCD → Elements.OnCircle A ABCD → Elements.OnCircle D ABCD → Elements.Between A E D → Elements.Between E F D → And (∀ (B : Elements.Point), Elements.OnCircle B ABCD → Ne B A → LT.lt (Elements.len F B) (Elements.len F A)) (And (∀ (G : Elements.Point), Elements.OnCircle G ABCD → Ne G D → LT.lt (Elements.len F D) (Elements.len F G)) (And (∀ (B C : Elements.Point), Elements.OnCircle B ABCD → Elements.OnCircle C ABCD → Not (Elements.Collinear A D B) → Not (Elements.Collinear A D C) → LT.lt (Elements.ang A F B) (Elements.ang A F C) → LT.lt (Elements.len F C) (Elements.len F B)) (∀ (G : Elements.Point), Elements.OnCircle G ABCD → Not (Elements.Collinear A D G) → Exists fun (H : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.OnCircle H ABCD) (And (Elements.OppositeSidesOf H G A D) (And (Eq (Elements.len F H) (Elements.len F G)) (∀ (K : Elements.Point), Elements.OnCircle K ABCD → Eq (Elements.len F K) (Elements.len F G) → Or (Eq K G) (Eq K H)))))))
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop7.general
propositions.enunciation:
**III.7, general** (companion of III.7). F is on the diameter AD of the circle ABCD with
centre E, strictly between E and D, so not the centre. Of the straight lines from F to the
circle, FA, the one through the centre, is greater than every other; FD, the rest of the
diameter, is less than every other. Of any two straight lines FB, FC whose ends B, C are off
the diameter, on one side of it or on opposite sides, the one making the less angle with the
ray FA at F is the greater: if the angle AFB is less than the angle AFC, then FC is less than
FB. Each point G of the circle off the diameter has one partner H on the other side with FH
equal to FG, and no third point of the circle is as far from F.

propositions.statement: ∀ {A D G : Elements.Point} {ABC : Elements.Circle}, Elements.OutsideCircle D ABC → Elements.OnCircle A ABC → Elements.OnCircle G ABC → Elements.Between D G A → (∀ (M : Elements.Point), Elements.Centre M ABC → Elements.Between G M A) → And (∀ (E : Elements.Point), Elements.OnCircle E ABC → Ne E A → LT.lt (Elements.len D E) (Elements.len D A)) (And (∀ (E F : Elements.Point), Elements.OnCircle E ABC → Elements.OnCircle F ABC → (Exists fun (H : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.OnCircle H ABC) (Elements.Between D H E)) → (Exists fun (L : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.OnCircle L ABC) (Elements.Between D L F)) → Not (Elements.Collinear D A E) → Not (Elements.Collinear D A F) → LT.lt (Elements.ang A D E) (Elements.ang A D F) → LT.lt (Elements.len D F) (Elements.len D E)) (And (∀ (K : Elements.Point), Elements.OnCircle K ABC → Ne K G → LT.lt (Elements.len D G) (Elements.len D K)) (And (∀ (K L : Elements.Point), Elements.OnCircle K ABC → Elements.OnCircle L ABC → (Exists fun (C : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.OnCircle C ABC) (Elements.Between D K C)) → (Exists fun (F : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.OnCircle F ABC) (Elements.Between D L F)) → Not (Elements.Collinear D A K) → Not (Elements.Collinear D A L) → LT.lt (Elements.ang A D K) (Elements.ang A D L) → LT.lt (Elements.len D K) (Elements.len D L)) (∀ (K : Elements.Point), Elements.OnCircle K ABC → Not (Elements.Collinear D A K) → Exists fun (B : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.OnCircle B ABC) (And (Elements.OppositeSidesOf B K D A) (And (Eq (Elements.len D B) (Elements.len D K)) (∀ (N : Elements.Point), Elements.OnCircle N ABC → Eq (Elements.len D N) (Elements.len D K) → Or (Eq N K) (Eq N B))))))))
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop8.general
propositions.enunciation:
**III.8, general** (companion of III.8). D is outside the circle ABC, and the straight
line DA passes through the centre, meeting the circle first at G and again at A. Of the
straight lines from D to the circle, DA is greater than every other, and DG less than every
other. Of any two points E, F of the concave circumference (each with a point of the circle
between it and D) off DA, on one side of it or on opposite sides, the one making the less
angle with the ray DA at D is the farther: if the angle ADE is less than the angle ADF, then
DF is less than DE. Of any two points K, L of the convex circumference (each with a point of
the circle beyond it) off DA, the one making the less angle is the nearer: if the angle ADK
is less than the angle ADL, then DK is less than DL. By convention, read from "drawn
through", a point where a straight line from D touches the circle is on neither
circumference; the comparisons speak only of points with a point of the circle before them
or beyond them, and that a point of contact has neither, which follows from Definition III.2,
is not stated here. Each point K of the circle off DA has one partner B on the other side
with DB equal to DK, and no third point of the circle is as far from D.

propositions.statement: ∀ {α β : Elements.Circle} {C : Elements.Point}, Iff (Elements.CirclesTouch α β C) (Elements.CirclesTouchAt α β C)
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop13.circlesTouch_iff
propositions.enunciation:
**The two readings of Definition III.3 agree**, for any two circles: the circles touch at
C, read of the whole circles, exactly when they touch at C, read at the point.

propositions.statement: ∀ {α β : Elements.Circle} {C : Elements.Point}, Iff (Elements.TouchesExternally α β C) (Elements.TouchesExternallyAt α β C)
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop13.touchesExternally_iff
propositions.enunciation: **The two readings of contact without agree**, for any two circles.

propositions.statement: ∀ {α β : Elements.Circle} {C : Elements.Point}, Iff (Elements.TouchesInternally α β C) (Elements.TouchesInternallyAt α β C)
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop13.touchesInternally_iff
propositions.enunciation: **The two readings of contact within agree**, for any two circles.

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B C D E F G : Elements.Point} {ABDC : Elements.Circle}, Elements.Centre E ABDC → Elements.OnCircle A ABDC → Elements.OnCircle B ABDC → Elements.OnCircle C ABDC → Elements.OnCircle D ABDC → Ne A B → Ne C D → Elements.Foot E A B F → Elements.Foot E C D G → Iff (Eq (Elements.len A B) (Elements.len C D)) (Eq (Elements.len E F) (Elements.len E G))
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop14.general
propositions.enunciation:
**III.14, general** (companion of III.14). In a circle, straight lines AB, CD are equal
exactly when they are equally distant from the centre E: EF and EG are equal, F and G being
the feet of the perpendiculars from E. Two straight lines not through the centre are
Euclid's case [III. 14]; two diameters are equal, and both at no distance; and of a diameter
and a straight line not through the centre, the diameter is the greater [I. 20], and the
other is at some distance from the centre.

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B C D E : Elements.Point} {ABCD : Elements.Circle}, Elements.Centre E ABCD → Elements.OnCircle A ABCD → Elements.OnCircle D ABCD → Elements.Between A E D → Elements.OnCircle B ABCD → Elements.OnCircle C ABCD → And (LE.le (Elements.len B C) (Elements.len A D)) (Iff (Eq (Elements.len B C) (Elements.len A D)) (Elements.Between B E C))
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop15.le_diameter
propositions.enunciation:
**III.15, the diameter is greatest** (companion of III.15). Of the straight lines in a
circle, none is greater than the diameter AD, and a straight line BC in it is equal to the
diameter exactly when it passes through the centre E: when it is a diameter too. If BC is
not through the centre, BE, EC together are greater than BC [I. 20], and they are equal to
AD. BC may be a point, and then it is nothing.

propositions.statement: ∀ {B C E F G H K : Elements.Point} {ABCD : Elements.Circle}, Elements.Centre E ABCD → Elements.OnCircle B ABCD → Elements.OnCircle C ABCD → Elements.OnCircle F ABCD → Elements.OnCircle G ABCD → Ne B C → Elements.Foot E B C H → Elements.Foot E F G K → LT.lt (Elements.len E H) (Elements.len E K) → LT.lt (Elements.len F G) (Elements.len B C)
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop15.nearer
propositions.enunciation:
**III.15, the nearer is greater** (companion of III.15). Of two straight lines BC, FG in
a circle, the one nearer to the centre E is the greater: if EH is less than EK, H and K being
the feet of the perpendiculars from E, then FG is less than BC. The nearer, BC, may be a
diameter, at no distance; the more remote cannot be. (Nor can FG be a point: its foot would
be E, and EK nothing.)

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B D E X Y Z : Elements.Point} {ABC : Elements.Circle}, Elements.Centre D ABC → Elements.OnCircle A ABC → Elements.Between A D B → Not (Elements.Collinear A B E) → Eq (Elements.ang B A E) Elements.rightAngle → Elements.Triangle X Y Z → LT.lt (Elements.ang X Y Z) Elements.rightAngle → And (Exists fun (F : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.SameSideOf F E A B) (And (Eq (Elements.ang B A F) (Elements.ang X Y Z)) (Elements.MixedAngle.Exceeds (Elements.MixedAngle.ofSegment A B ABC E) B F))) (Exists fun (F : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.SameSideOf F B A E) (And (Eq (Elements.ang E A F) (Elements.ang X Y Z)) (Elements.MixedAngle.FallsShort (Elements.MixedAngle.ofContact A E ABC B) E F)))
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop16.acute
propositions.enunciation:
**III.16, for any acute rectilineal angle.** Every acute rectilineal angle XYZ can be
placed at A [I. 23]: along AB on E's side, where the angle of the semicircle exceeds it, and
along AE on the circle's side, where the remaining angle falls short of it. A copy placed
so compares as any other (`WithinAngle.locallyLess_placement`).

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B D E : Elements.Point} {ABC : Elements.Circle}, Elements.Centre D ABC → Elements.OnCircle A ABC → Elements.Between A D B → Not (Elements.Collinear A B E) → Eq (Elements.ang B A E) Elements.rightAngle → And (Elements.MixedAngle.WellFormed (Elements.MixedAngle.ofContact A E ABC B)) (∀ (F : Elements.Point), Elements.SameSideOf F B A E → LT.lt (Elements.ang E A F) Elements.rightAngle → Elements.MixedAngle.FallsShort (Elements.MixedAngle.ofContact A E ABC B) E F)
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop16.remaining
propositions.enunciation:
**III.16: the remaining angle is less than any acute rectilineal angle.** In Euclid's
figure, the remaining angle, contained by the circumference and the straight line AE, is a
mixed angle as Euclid draws it, and it falls short of every acute angle EAF placed at A
along AE on the circle's side. Every acute rectilineal angle can be placed so
(`Prop16.acute`).

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B D E : Elements.Point} {ABC : Elements.Circle}, Elements.Centre D ABC → Elements.OnCircle A ABC → Elements.Between A D B → Not (Elements.Collinear A B E) → Eq (Elements.ang B A E) Elements.rightAngle → And (Elements.MixedAngle.WellFormed (Elements.MixedAngle.ofSegment A B ABC E)) (∀ (F : Elements.Point), Elements.SameSideOf F E A B → LT.lt (Elements.ang B A F) Elements.rightAngle → Elements.MixedAngle.Exceeds (Elements.MixedAngle.ofSegment A B ABC E) B F)
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop16.semicircle
propositions.enunciation:
**III.16: the angle of the semicircle is greater than any acute rectilineal angle.** In
Euclid's figure, the circle ABC about D with the diameter AB and AE at right angles to it,
the angle of the semicircle, contained by the straight line BA and the circumference on E's
side, is a mixed angle as Euclid draws it, and it exceeds every acute angle BAF placed at A
along AB on that side. Every acute rectilineal angle can be placed so (`Prop16.acute`).

propositions.statement: ∀ {A : Elements.Point} {BCD : Elements.Circle}, Not (Elements.InsideCircle A BCD) → Exists fun (X : Elements.Point) => Elements.Touches A X BCD
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop17.general
propositions.enunciation:
**III.17, general** (companion of III.17). Given a circle BCD and a point
A not within it, there is a point X such that the straight line AX touches the circle: it
meets the circle, and does not cut it. A may be outside the circle, and then the point of
contact is another point (Euclid's case, `Prop17`); or on it, and then the point of
contact is A itself: the proof draws AX at right angles to the radius EA (I.11), and it
touches by III.16's porism. Euclid leaves that case out, Heath explains, because III.16's
porism so directly indicates its construction (vol. 2, p. 44); the construction is not on
Euclid's page.

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B D E X Y Z : Elements.Point} {ABC : Elements.Circle}, Elements.Centre D ABC → Elements.OnCircle A ABC → Elements.Touches A E ABC → Elements.Between A D B → Elements.Triangle X Y Z → LT.lt (Elements.ang X Y Z) Elements.rightAngle → And (Elements.MixedAngle.WellFormed (Elements.MixedAngle.ofSegment A B ABC E)) (And (Elements.MixedAngle.WellFormed (Elements.MixedAngle.ofContact A E ABC B)) (And (Exists fun (F : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.SameSideOf F E A B) (And (Eq (Elements.ang B A F) (Elements.ang X Y Z)) (Elements.MixedAngle.Exceeds (Elements.MixedAngle.ofSegment A B ABC E) B F))) (Exists fun (F : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.SameSideOf F B A E) (And (Eq (Elements.ang E A F) (Elements.ang X Y Z)) (Elements.MixedAngle.FallsShort (Elements.MixedAngle.ofContact A E ABC B) E F)))))
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop18.acute
propositions.enunciation:
**III.16's last clause, for every straight line touching a circle.** Let AE touch the
circle ABC, about D, at A, and AB be the diameter through A; for the angle of the semicircle,
AE only names the side of AB (`Prop18.semicircle_gt`). The angle of the semicircle and
the angle of contact are angles as Euclid draws them, and every acute rectilineal angle XYZ
can be placed at A [I. 23]: along AB on E's side, where the angle of the semicircle exceeds
it, and along AE on the circle's side, where the angle of contact falls short of it. Once
III.18 makes AE III.16's straight line (`Prop18.diameter`), the placing and the comparisons
are III.16's own, cited from its companion `Prop16.acute`.

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B B' E : Elements.Point} {ABC : Elements.Circle}, Elements.MixedAngle.WellFormed (Elements.MixedAngle.ofContact A E ABC B) → Elements.MixedAngle.WellFormed (Elements.MixedAngle.ofContact A E ABC B') → Elements.LocallyEqual A (Elements.MixedAngle.region (Elements.MixedAngle.ofContact A E ABC B)) (Elements.MixedAngle.region (Elements.MixedAngle.ofContact A E ABC B'))
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop18.contact_locallyEqual
propositions.enunciation:
**The angle of contact does not depend on the straight line that names its branch.** Let
AE touch a circle at A, and let D be its centre (`Tacit.exists_centre`). Any two angles of
contact along AE, each with its branch
named by a straight line from A into the circle, are equal near A: each is, near A, the
angle of contact of III.16's figure, named by the diameter through A.

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B E F : Elements.Point} {ABC : Elements.Circle}, Elements.MixedAngle.WellFormed (Elements.MixedAngle.ofContact A E ABC B) → Elements.SameSideOf F B A E → LT.lt (Elements.ang E A F) Elements.rightAngle → Elements.MixedAngle.FallsShort (Elements.MixedAngle.ofContact A E ABC B) E F
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop18.contact_lt
propositions.enunciation:
**The angle of contact is less than any acute rectilineal angle**, for every straight line
touching a circle. Let AE touch a circle at A, let D be its centre (`Tacit.exists_centre`),
and let B name the branch of the angle of contact by a straight line from A into the circle.
For every acute angle EAF placed at A
along AE, on the circle's side, the angle of contact falls short of it. By III.18 the
diameter AB₀ through A is at right angles to AE, and III.16's remaining angle, named by B₀,
falls short of EAF (`Prop16.horn_lt`); the angle named by B is the same near A
(`Prop18.branch`).

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B D E F : Elements.Point} {ABC : Elements.Circle}, Elements.Centre D ABC → Elements.OnCircle A ABC → Elements.Touches A E ABC → Elements.Between A D B → Elements.SameSideOf F E A B → LT.lt (Elements.ang B A F) Elements.rightAngle → Elements.MixedAngle.Exceeds (Elements.MixedAngle.ofSegment A B ABC E) B F
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop18.semicircle_gt
propositions.enunciation:
**The angle of the semicircle is greater than any acute rectilineal angle**, on the side
of the diameter that a touching straight line names. Let AE touch the circle ABC, about D, at
A, and AB be the diameter through A. For every acute angle BAF placed at A along AB, on E's
side, the angle of the semicircle, contained by the straight line BA and the circumference on
E's side, exceeds it: by III.18 this is III.16's figure (`Prop16.semicircle_gt`). The
touching straight line AE only names the side of AB. The angle of the semicircle does not
depend on it, and on any side of the diameter the comparison follows from III.16, with the
perpendicular to AB at A drawn on that side by I.11. III.16's companion `Prop16.semicircle`
states that form, with AE at right angles to AB.

propositions.statement: ∀ {B C K : Elements.Point} {α : Elements.Circle}, Elements.OnCircle B α → Elements.OnCircle C α → Elements.Triangle B C K → Eq (Elements.circumference α B K C) (Elements.angleAtCentre α B K C)
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop20.circumference
propositions.enunciation:
**The circumference is its angle at the centre.** Our measure of the circumference
BKC, `circumference`, is twice the angle at some point of the circle on the other side of
BC. That is the angle at the centre standing on it, in every case: less than a
semicircle, a semicircle, or greater. Of III.20–III.22 it needs III.20 alone, where
`Circumference.eq` needs III.21; `Circumference.centre`, for the circumference beyond
which the centre lies, is a case of it. [III. 2, III. 20]

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B C E : Elements.Point} {ABC : Elements.Circle}, Elements.Centre E ABC → Elements.OnCircle A ABC → Elements.OnCircle B ABC → Elements.OnCircle C ABC → Elements.SameSideOf E A B C → Eq (Elements.ang B E C) (HAdd.hAdd (Elements.ang B A C) (Elements.ang B A C))
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop20.special
propositions.enunciation:
**III.20, the centre on A's side of BC.** Then the angle BEC is double of the angle
BAC: the angle at the centre standing on the circumference on the other side is the angle
BEC itself (`angleAtCentre.within`), less than two right angles, as Euclid's angles at
the centre are. It follows from the general statement, for the propositions that ask
only for the angle BEC.

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B E P : Elements.Point} {α : Elements.Circle}, Elements.OnCircle A α → Elements.OnCircle B α → Elements.OnCircle E α → Elements.SameSideOf P E A B → And (Iff (Elements.OnCircle P α) (Eq (Elements.ang A P B) (Elements.ang A E B))) (Iff (Elements.InsideCircle P α) (LT.lt (Elements.ang A E B) (Elements.ang A P B)))
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop23.point
propositions.enunciation:
**On the circle, by the angle.** Let A, B, E be points of a circle, and P a
point on E's side of AB. Then P is on the circle exactly when the angle APB is equal to the
angle AEB, and P is within the circle exactly when the angle APB is greater than the angle
AEB.

Proved through a point M between A and B, which is within the circle [III. 2]. On the circle,
the angles in the same segment are equal [III. 21]. Outside it, the finite straight line PM
meets the circle at a point Q, which is within the triangle ABP, so the angle AQB is greater
than the angle APB [I. 21]. Within it, MP produced beyond P meets the circle at a point Q,
and P is within the triangle ABQ, so the angle APB is greater than the angle AQB [I. 21]. In
both, Q is on E's side of AB, and the angle AQB is equal to the angle AEB [III. 21]. (A plan
that draws AP on fails when AP touches the circle at A.)

A companion of III.23 ("III.23 point"): its content, point by point. III.24 cites it.

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B C D E F : Elements.Point} {AEB CFD : Elements.Circle}, Elements.OnCircle A AEB → Elements.OnCircle B AEB → Elements.OnCircle E AEB → Elements.OnCircle C CFD → Elements.OnCircle D CFD → Elements.OnCircle F CFD → Not (Elements.Collinear A B E) → Not (Elements.Collinear C D F) → Eq (Elements.len A B) (Elements.len C D) → Eq (Elements.ang A E B) (Elements.ang C F D) → And (Elements.EqualCircles AEB CFD) (Eq (Elements.circumference AEB A E B) (Elements.circumference CFD C F D))
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop24.equalCircles
propositions.enunciation:
**III.24, the circles and the measures** (companion of III.24, "III.24 equalCircles").
Similar segments on equal straight lines lie in equal circles, and their circumferences are
equal in measure. This is the proof by the radii (the angles at the centres, III.20 and
III.22, and isosceles triangles on the equal bases, `Prop24.isosceles`), an alternative to
Euclid's application of one segment to the other, and labelled so on the page, with
Euclid's text in full under the main proof. The measures follow from the equal angles
alone; the equal bases are needed for the circles. `Arc.congruent_iff` cites it for the
equal circles.

propositions.statement: ∀ {a b : Elements.Arc}, Elements.Arc.Drawn a → Elements.Arc.Drawn b → Elements.Arc.Congruent a b → Eq (Elements.Arc.measure a) (Elements.Arc.measure b)
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop24.equalMeasure
propositions.enunciation:
**Congruent segments have equal circumferences** (companion of III.24, "III.24
equalMeasure"). If two drawn segments are congruent, their circumferences are equal in
measure. III.26 cites it after III.24, where Euclid passes from the equal segments to the
equal circumferences [III. 24]; nothing before III.26 says it otherwise, for `Arc.congruent_iff`
comes after III.29.

Proved: take a point P of the first arc off its base (`Prop2.sameSide`, by III.2); its
image is a point of the second arc, off its base (it is neither end, being as far from each
as P is, and `Prop24.chord_cases`); the congruence keeps the distances from P to the ends, so the
angle at P is the angle at its image [I. 8] (these steps are `Prop24.image`); the
circumference on the other side of each base is twice that angle (`Circumference.eq`), and
with it each circumference makes up the whole circle (`Circumference.whole`); so the
circumferences are equal [C.N. 3].

propositions.statement: ∀ {A C P B : Elements.Point} {α γ : Elements.Circle}, Elements.OnCircle A α → Elements.OnCircle C α → Elements.OnArc B (Elements.Arc.mk α A C P) → Elements.SameSideOf B P A C → Elements.OnCircle A γ → Elements.OnCircle B γ → Elements.OnCircle C γ → And (Eq γ α) (∀ (X : Elements.Point), Elements.OnArc X (Elements.Arc.mk α A C P) → Elements.OnCircle X γ)
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop25.complete
propositions.enunciation:
**III.25's circle is the segment's circle.** Let A, C be points of a circle α,
and B a point of its arc on P's side of AC (B on P's side). Any circle γ
through A, B and C is α, and every point of the arc AC on P's side is on γ.

A companion of III.25 ("III.25 complete"): its correctness argument, kept apart from the
construction core. It carries Heath's "of which it is a segment", and Euclid's step
"[III. 9]": the rule gives a centre E of γ; A, B and C are three points of α on γ,
so EA, EB, EC are equal, E is the centre of α, and one centre with one radius makes one
circle (`circle_eq`). [III. 9]

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B C D E P : Elements.Point} {γ : Elements.Circle}, Elements.SameSideOf B P A C → Elements.Between A D C → Elements.Centre E γ → Elements.OnCircle A γ → Elements.OnCircle C γ → (LT.lt (Elements.ang B A D) (Elements.ang A B D) → Elements.OppositeSidesOf E B A C) → (Eq (Elements.ang A B D) (Elements.ang B A D) → Eq E D) → (LT.lt (Elements.ang A B D) (Elements.ang B A D) → Elements.SameSideOf E B A C) → And (Elements.Arc.Drawn (Elements.Arc.mk γ A C P)) (And (LT.lt (Elements.ang B A D) (Elements.ang A B D) → And (Elements.Arc.Less (Elements.Arc.mk γ A C P)) (LT.lt (Elements.circumference γ A P C) (HAdd.hAdd Elements.rightAngle Elements.rightAngle))) (And (Eq (Elements.ang A B D) (Elements.ang B A D) → And (Elements.Arc.Semicircle (Elements.Arc.mk γ A C P)) (Eq (Elements.circumference γ A P C) (HAdd.hAdd Elements.rightAngle Elements.rightAngle))) (LT.lt (Elements.ang A B D) (Elements.ang B A D) → And (Elements.Arc.Greater (Elements.Arc.mk γ A C P)) (LT.lt (HAdd.hAdd Elements.rightAngle Elements.rightAngle) (Elements.circumference γ A P C)))))
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop25.kind
propositions.enunciation:
The centre's position in III.25 determines whether the segment is less than a
semicircle, a semicircle or greater, and how its circumference compares with two right angles.
B is on P's side of AC, and D lies between A and C. The construction's three conclusions
place E across AC from B, at D, or on B's side. `Prop25.complete` identifies the constructed
circle with the given segment's circle, carrying these conclusions to that segment.
[I. 5, I. 32, III. 2, III. 20, III. 21, III. 22]

propositions.statement: ∀ {A C : Elements.Point} {ABC : Elements.Circle}, Elements.OnCircle A ABC → Elements.OnCircle C ABC → ∀ (P : Elements.Point), Not (Elements.Collinear A C P) → Exists fun (B : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (D : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (E : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.OnCircle B ABC) (And (Elements.SameSideOf B P A C) (And (Elements.Between A D C) (And (Eq (Elements.len A D) (Elements.len D C)) (And (Eq (Elements.ang A D B) Elements.rightAngle) (And (Elements.Centre E ABC) (And (Elements.Collinear D B E) (And (LT.lt (Elements.ang B A D) (Elements.ang A B D) → Elements.OppositeSidesOf E B A C) (And (Eq (Elements.ang A B D) (Elements.ang B A D) → Eq E D) (LT.lt (Elements.ang A B D) (Elements.ang B A D) → Elements.SameSideOf E B A C)))))))))
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop25.of_circle
propositions.enunciation:
**III.25, handed the whole circle** (companion of III.25, "III.25 of_circle"). Handed
the circle ABC, the core run on the points of its arc on P's side (which meet every
straight line from within the base, by `Prop25.meets`) finds a circle that is ABC itself
(`Prop25.complete`), so its centre E is the centre of ABC. This is III.25's statement
before brief 0006 restated it, with the centre-existence hypothesis removed (the `example`
below checks it against that statement); it retains its certificate. Proved from the core,
`Prop25.meets` and `Prop25.complete`, it checks that the pieces fit.

propositions.statement: ∀ {A B D P : Elements.Point} {ADB : Elements.Circle}, Elements.OnCircle A ADB → Elements.OnCircle B ADB → Elements.OnCircle D ADB → Elements.SameSideOf D P A B → Eq (Elements.standing ADB A B D) (Elements.standing ADB D A B) → Exists fun (Q : Elements.Point) => Exists fun (R : Elements.Point) => And (Elements.OppositeSidesOf Q B A D) (And (Elements.OppositeSidesOf R A D B) (And (Elements.Arc.Drawn (Elements.Arc.mk ADB A D Q)) (And (Elements.Arc.Drawn (Elements.Arc.mk ADB D B R)) (And (Elements.Arc.Congruent (Elements.Arc.mk ADB A D Q) (Elements.Arc.mk ADB D B R)) (And (Eq (HAdd.hAdd (Elements.circumference ADB A Q D) (Elements.circumference ADB D R B)) (Elements.circumference ADB A P B)) (And (∀ (X : Elements.Point), Iff (Elements.OnArc X (Elements.Arc.mk ADB A B P)) (Or (Elements.OnArc X (Elements.Arc.mk ADB A D Q)) (Elements.OnArc X (Elements.Arc.mk ADB D B R)))) (∀ (X : Elements.Point), Iff (And (Elements.OnArc X (Elements.Arc.mk ADB A D Q)) (Elements.OnArc X (Elements.Arc.mk ADB D B R))) (Eq X D))))))))
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop30.halves
propositions.enunciation:
**III.30's halves** (companion of III.30, "III.30 halves"). Let D be a point of the
circle ADB on P's side of AB, with the circumferences standing at B and at A equal, as
III.30 finds it. Then the circumference AD away from B, named by Q, and the circumference DB
away from A, named by R, are drawn and congruent; together they make up the given
circumference AB on P's side; every point of it lies on one or the other; and the two share
only D, ends included.

III.30's statement gives the equal measures, not the equal straight lines AD, DB that its
proof finds by I.4, so they are recovered here: the equal measures are twice the angles
ABD, DAB (`Circumference.standing`), so those angles are equal, and DA is equal to DB
[I. 6]. Each circumference is less than a semicircle [I. 17], so III.28's congruence of the
less circumferences applies. They add by `Circumference.add`, and the division point by
point follows from III.2 (`Prop30.on_chord`, `Prop30.not_within`, `Prop30.not_vertical`).
[I. 6, I. 17, III. 2, III. 28]

propositions.statement: ∀ {A C E : Elements.Point} {ABCD : Elements.Circle}, Elements.Centre E ABCD → Elements.OnCircle A ABCD → Elements.OnCircle C ABCD → Not (Elements.Collinear A C E) → And (Elements.MixedAngle.WellFormed (Elements.MixedAngle.ofSegment A C ABCD E)) (∀ (R : Elements.Point), Elements.SameSideOf R E A C → Eq (Elements.ang C A R) Elements.rightAngle → Elements.MixedAngle.Exceeds (Elements.MixedAngle.ofSegment A C ABCD E) C R)
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop31.greater
propositions.enunciation:
**III.31: the angle of the greater segment is greater than a right angle.** For any
straight line AC in the circle ABCD about E, not through the centre, at either end A: the
angle of the segment on the centre's side, the greater segment, is a mixed angle as Euclid
draws it, and it exceeds every right angle CAR placed along AC on that side. Euclid's figure
is the case where B, the far end of the diameter through C, names the segment
(`Prop31.diameter_through`).

propositions.statement: ∀ {A C D E : Elements.Point} {ABCD : Elements.Circle}, Elements.Centre E ABCD → Elements.OnCircle A ABCD → Elements.OnCircle C ABCD → Not (Elements.Collinear A C E) → Elements.OppositeSidesOf E D A C → And (Elements.MixedAngle.WellFormed (Elements.MixedAngle.ofSegment A C ABCD D)) (∀ (R : Elements.Point), Elements.SameSideOf R D A C → Eq (Elements.ang C A R) Elements.rightAngle → Elements.MixedAngle.FallsShort (Elements.MixedAngle.ofSegment A C ABCD D) C R)
propositions.name: BookIII.Prop31.less
propositions.enunciation:
**III.31: the angle of the less segment is less than a right angle.** For any straight
line AC in the circle ABCD about E, not through the centre, at either end A, and a point D on
the other side of AC from the centre: the angle of the segment on D's side, the less segment,
is a mixed angle as Euclid draws it, and it falls short of every right angle CAR placed along
AC on that side.
